Oncology clinic follow-up for a 78-year-old female with stage I, estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, status post lumpectomy and radiation, who is 18 months into a planned five years of adjuvant endocrine therapy with anastrozole. Other conditions include hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. She has no known drug allergies. This is her first visit since a four-day hospital stay about three weeks ago after a fall at home, which caused a left distal radius fracture that was repaired surgically. Her adult daughter came with her and helped with the history.

The patient has limited health literacy and told us she has trouble reading labels, so I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout. When asked how she takes her medicines, she first said she takes anastrozole 2 mg every morning because she takes "two little pills." Her daughter had brought every pill bottle in a bag, and when we read the labels together the anastrozole is 1 mg, one tablet once daily, and the second pill she meant is her levothyroxine. She also first said metformin 1000 mg twice a day, but the bottle reads metformin 500 mg twice daily. The corrected regimen is anastrozole 1 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. She was sent home from the hospital on ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for wrist pain and has taken it nearly every day since.

She reports mild joint aches in her hands and knees that are worse in the morning, occasional hot flashes, and wrist pain that is slowly improving. She denies a new breast lump, nipple discharge, bone pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, fever, black stools, and stomach pain.

On examination, blood pressure is 148/86, heart rate 78, temperature 36.8 C, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Weight is 68 kg. The right breast lumpectomy scar is well healed with no mass, and the left breast has no mass. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy on either side. The left wrist incision is clean and dry without redness or drainage, and she has full finger motion. Lungs are clear and the heart rhythm is regular. The abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Labs drawn today show creatinine 1.2 mg/dL with eGFR 49, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, TSH 2.1, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 19 ng/mL. A bone density scan done during the hospital stay showed a lumbar spine T-score of -2.9. Her last screening mammogram of the left breast, done about four months ago, was negative.

Impression: stage I breast cancer on adjuvant anastrozole with no clinical sign of recurrence and mild joint aches and hot flashes from the aromatase inhibitor; osteoporosis with a fragility fracture; regular ibuprofen use in the setting of stage 3a chronic kidney disease and hypertension, which is unsafe; blood pressure above goal; and medication confusion related to limited health literacy.

Plan: continue anastrozole 1 mg once daily and encourage walking and stretching for the joint aches. Stop ibuprofen today and use acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed for wrist pain. Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly after a dental check, with teaching to take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for 30 minutes, and start vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily, and her daughter will check blood pressure at home and bring the log. Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily and levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. Repeat a basic metabolic panel in two weeks to recheck kidney function off ibuprofen. The clinic pharmacist will prepare a pill organizer with her daughter and a one-page picture medication list, and the nurse will call in one week to check understanding. Orthopedic follow-up continues as scheduled. A social worker will see her today about transportation and home support. Return to clinic in three months, sooner for new breast changes, bone pain, or black stools.

She has limited health literacy, and review of her pill bottles corrected the anastrozole and metformin doses she first reported. Blood pressure was 148/86, there was no breast mass or lymphadenopathy, and she has osteoporosis, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, and regular ibuprofen use. Ibuprofen was stopped, alendronate and vitamin D3 were started, and amlodipine was increased from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Pharmacist, nurse, and social work support were arranged.

Endocrinology clinic visit for a 61-year-old male referred for evaluation of an incidental right adrenal nodule. The nodule was found on a CT of the abdomen done in the emergency department three months ago for flank pain from a kidney stone, which he has since passed. It measures 3.2 cm with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units. His only chronic condition is hypertension, treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily.

He denies headaches, palpitations, spells of sweating, easy bruising, muscle weakness, and weight gain.

Blood pressure today is 132/80 and heart rate is 70. On exam he has no facial plethora, no purple striae, and no muscle weakness in the proximal muscles. Work-up so far: an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test gave a morning cortisol of 1.2 mcg/dL, which is normal suppression. Plasma free metanephrines were within normal limits. Serum potassium is 4.2, and I do not suspect primary aldosteronism.

Impression: 3.2 cm right adrenal incidentaloma with benign imaging features, hormonally nonfunctioning on the testing above, with no evidence of pheochromocytoma or autonomous cortisol secretion. His hypertension appears essential.

Plan: no surgery is needed, and no further adrenal imaging is required because the nodule is under 4 cm with a benign attenuation. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily through primary care. I reviewed the results with him and he understands. He should return to clinic only if he develops new headaches, palpitations, or sweating spells, or if his blood pressure becomes hard to control.

Dexamethasone suppression testing, plasma free metanephrines, and serum potassium were normal, and the nodule has benign imaging features. Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 26-year-old male here about acne on your face and back. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah, I keep getting breakouts on my forehead, cheeks, and upper back. It's been going on for about two years and it's getting worse.
Doctor: Any big painful lumps under the skin, or scarring?
Patient: No, no big painful ones. Just a lot of red bumps and whiteheads. I've got a few dark spots left over where they healed.
Doctor: Have you tried anything for it?
Patient: Just a regular drugstore face wash. It doesn't do much.
Doctor: Do you take any medications or supplements, like protein powders or steroids? And any allergies?
Patient: No, nothing. No steroids, no supplements, and no allergies.
Doctor: Any family history of bad acne?
Patient: My brother had it pretty bad in high school.
Doctor: Okay, let me take a look. On your forehead and cheeks you have a lot of open and closed comedones, with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules. Your upper back looks the same. I don't see any nodules or cysts, and no significant scarring, just some mild dark marks left behind.
Patient: So what can I do about it?
Doctor: This is mild to moderate acne vulgaris. I'd like to start adapalene 0.1% gel, a pea-sized amount on the affected areas every night after washing. In the morning, use benzoyl peroxide 5% gel on those same areas. Expect some dryness and peeling at first, so use a gentle moisturizer and a sunscreen during the day, and don't pick at the spots.
Patient: How long until I see a difference?
Doctor: Usually about eight to twelve weeks. I'll see you back then, and if it hasn't improved enough we'll talk about other options.
Patient: Sounds good.

He denies big painful lumps and scarring, takes no medications or supplements, and has no allergies. Exam showed open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules, and a few pustules without nodules, cysts, or significant scarring. The diagnosis is mild to moderate acne vulgaris. He was started on adapalene 0.1% gel every night and benzoyl peroxide 5% gel every morning, with moisturizer and sunscreen advice and follow-up in eight to twelve weeks.

Chief Complaint: Shortness of breath and wheezing.

HPI: 19-year-old male with asthma since childhood who presents with one day of worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, and a dry cough. This followed two days of nasal congestion and sore throat. He used his albuterol inhaler about every hour overnight with only brief relief and came in because he could not finish a sentence. He also reports a racing heart. He first told the triage nurse that he takes his controller inhaler, fluticasone-salmeterol, twice a day, but on further questioning he admitted he ran out about three months ago and has used only albuterol since then. He has had two ED visits for asthma in the past year, with no ICU stays and no intubations. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Past Medical History: asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema.

Medications: albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, fluticasone-salmeterol 100/50 mcg one inhalation twice daily (not taking), montelukast 10 mg nightly, cetirizine 10 mg daily. Over-the-counter supplements: a pre-workout powder containing caffeine and other stimulants, one scoop daily for two months, and creatine 5 g daily. No known drug allergies.

Social History: College student who lives with roommates. He first said he drinks a few beers a day, then corrected himself and said it is about 4 beers most nights and 10 to 12 on weekend nights, with his last drink about 14 hours ago. He denies tobacco, vaping, and other drug use.

ROS: Constitutional: no fever or chills. Cardiovascular: no chest pain or leg swelling. GI: no vomiting. Neurologic: no confusion. All other systems negative except as in the HPI.

Physical Exam: Vitals on arrival: temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 118, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 91% on room air, peak expiratory flow 220 L/min, about 40% of predicted. General: moderate respiratory distress, speaking in 3 to 4 word sentences. Lungs: diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase and decreased air movement at the bases; no stridor. CV: tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmur. Neck: trachea midline. Skin: dry eczematous patches in both antecubital fossae, no cyanosis. Neuro: alert and oriented, mild fine tremor of both hands, no asterixis.

ED Course and Results: Oxygen 2 L by nasal cannula was started. He received three back-to-back ipratropium-albuterol nebulizers, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, and magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. After treatment heart rate was 98, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and peak expiratory flow 340 L/min, about 62% of predicted. Labs: venous blood gas pH 7.38 and pCO2 41; WBC 11.8, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL; sodium 139, potassium 3.4, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, glucose 112 mg/dL; serum ethanol level undetectable. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 116 with normal intervals. Chest x-ray showed hyperinflated lungs without pneumothorax or consolidation. CIWA score was 2 with no signs of alcohol withdrawal.

Medical Decision Making: 19-year-old male with a moderate to severe acute asthma exacerbation, most likely triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and several months without controller therapy. The stimulant pre-workout supplement and repeated albuterol likely contribute to his racing heart and tremor. Pneumothorax and pneumonia are not supported by the chest x-ray, and pulmonary embolism is unlikely given no leg swelling and no pleuritic pain. He has heavy alcohol use, but the ethanol level is undetectable and he has no withdrawal signs.

Disposition: After four hours of observation he is speaking full sentences, oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, and peak expiratory flow is 400 L/min, about 73% of predicted. He is discharged home. Prescribed prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days. Fluticasone-salmeterol is restarted at a higher strength, increased from 100/50 mcg to 250/50 mcg, one inhalation twice daily, and he should rinse his mouth afterward. Continue albuterol HFA 2 to 4 puffs every 4 hours as needed with a spacer, montelukast 10 mg nightly, and cetirizine 10 mg daily. Stop the pre-workout supplement; creatine may be continued with plenty of water. Brief alcohol counseling was done and he was given resources for cutting down. Follow up with his primary care doctor in 2 to 3 days and the asthma clinic within 2 weeks. An asthma action plan was reviewed. Return for worsening breathing, needing albuterol more often than every 4 hours, or inability to speak in full sentences.
summary: A 19-year-old male with asthma presented with one day of worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, and cough after a viral illness, and he admitted he had been off his controller inhaler for three months. Doctor: Good morning. You're an 83-year-old male, and I understand your wife has been worried about your memory. Can you tell me what you've noticed?
Patient: Well, I don't think it's that bad. I forget where I put my glasses, and sometimes I lose the name of a person I've known for years.
Family member: It's more than that. He asks the same question three or four times in an hour, and he missed paying a couple of bills. It has been creeping up for about two years.
Doctor: Does he ever get lost when driving or walking around the neighborhood?
Family member: No, he only drives to the store and he's never gotten lost.
Doctor: Any hallucinations, like seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any falls, shaking, or trouble walking?
Family member: No falls, no shaking, and his walking is fine.
Doctor: Any head injury, or a sudden change that happened overnight?
Family member: No, it's been very slow.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my blood pressure, and I take Benadryl 25 mg at bedtime to help me sleep.
Doctor: Okay. Today your memory test, the MoCA, was 21 out of 30, and you lost points on delayed recall and the clock drawing. Your blood pressure is 138 over 78, and your strength, reflexes, and walking look normal, with no tremor or stiffness.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: My impression is mild dementia, most likely early Alzheimer's disease, but I want to rule out other causes first. I'd like to check a vitamin B12 level and a thyroid stimulating hormone level, and get an MRI of the brain without contrast. Benadryl can make memory worse in older adults, so I'd like you to stop it. Keep taking the amlodipine. We'll meet again in six weeks to go over the results and talk about treatment options.
Family member: Thank you, that's helpful.
Patient: Okay, I'll stop the Benadryl.
summary: An 83-year-old male presented with about two years of slowly progressive memory trouble, including forgetting where he puts things, repeating questions, and missing bills. He has had no getting lost, hallucinations, falls, shaking, or head injury, and he takes amlodipine and Benadryl at bedtime. His MoCA score was 21 out of 30, and his neurologic exam was normal. The impression is mild dementia, most likely early Alzheimer's disease. Vitamin B12, thyroid stimulating hormone, and a brain MRI were ordered, Benadryl was stopped, amlodipine continues, and follow-up is in six weeks.

Geriatrics progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is an 86-year-old female admitted after her third fall in two months, this time at night when she stood up from a chair to go to the bathroom. She denies loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, and new weakness, and she did not strike her head. She does report lightheadedness when she stands and gets up three to four times a night to urinate because of bladder urgency. A CT of the head on admission showed no bleeding, and a wrist X-ray showed only a bruise and no fracture.

Her home medication list was reviewed in detail because she takes nine medications. The ones most relevant to her falls are zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime for sleep, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for bladder urgency, and amlodipine 10 mg daily for hypertension. She also takes acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain.

Vitals this morning: lying blood pressure 146/80 with heart rate 72; after standing for three minutes blood pressure 112/64 with heart rate 76 and lightheadedness. Temperature 36.7 C and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On exam she is alert and oriented, lungs are clear, heart rhythm is regular, and there is no leg edema. Her gait is slow and wide-based and she needs a walker. Strength and sensation are intact and there are no focal deficits. Labs show creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, sodium 139, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, a normal vitamin B12, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 18 ng/mL. ECG showed sinus rhythm without block, and urinalysis was negative.

My impression is that these are recurrent falls that are multifactorial, with orthostatic hypotension, sedating and anticholinergic medications, bladder urgency causing nighttime trips to the bathroom, and vitamin D deficiency all contributing.

For management, stop zolpidem and use sleep hygiene measures. Stop oxybutynin and use timed voiding with fluids limited after dinner. Reduce amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg daily and repeat orthostatic vital signs in two days. Start vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Physical and occupational therapy will work on gait, transfers, and walker training, and a home safety evaluation will be done before discharge. Plan discharge once her orthostatic drop improves. Doctor: Good to see you again. You're a 45-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up, and I see you just got back from a trip. How was it?
Patient: It was great, thanks. I was in Kenya for three weeks visiting friends, and I got back about two weeks ago.
Doctor: Wonderful. Did you take your Biktarvy every day while you were away?
Patient: Yes, one tablet every morning. I only took it late once, about six hours late, because of the flight.
Doctor: That's fine. Did you take anything for malaria?
Patient: Yes, atovaquone-proguanil, one tablet daily. I started it two days before I left and finished it a week after I got home.
Doctor: Good. Any fever, chills, or sweats since you got back?
Patient: No fever, no chills, no night sweats.
Doctor: Any diarrhea or stomach trouble on the trip?
Patient: Yes, around the second week I had bad watery diarrhea for two days. I took azithromycin 500 mg once a day for three days that I got from a pharmacy there, and it cleared up. I also chewed Tums, two or three a day, for heartburn.
Doctor: Okay. The Tums matter, because calcium can bind to the Biktarvy and lower how much you absorb. We'll talk about that in a minute. Any cough, rash, weight loss, or yellow eyes?
Patient: No, none of those.
Doctor: Let me go over your other medicines. I have lisinopril 10 mg daily for blood pressure, atorvastatin for your high cholesterol, and omeprazole for reflux. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. The atorvastatin is 40 milligrams every evening.
Doctor: Our list says 20 milligrams. Can you check?
Patient: Hold on, let me look at the photo of the bottle on my phone. Oh, you're right, it's 20 milligrams every evening. I was thinking of my old dose.
Doctor: Thanks for checking. And the omeprazole?
Patient: 20 mg every morning, but honestly I haven't had heartburn in months except on the trip.
Doctor: Good to know. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or headaches?
Patient: No chest pain, no shortness of breath, just the occasional mild headache.
Doctor: Alright, here are your results from last week. Your viral load is undetectable, less than 20 copies per mL, your CD4 count is 612, creatinine 1.0, ALT 28, LDL 98, and A1c 5.6 percent. All of that looks great. Today your blood pressure is 146 over 88, and on the repeat it's 144 over 86. Heart rate is 74, temperature 36.7 Celsius, and weight is stable at 82 kilograms. I don't see any thrush, your lymph nodes are not enlarged, your lungs are clear, your abdomen is soft, and there's no rash.
Patient: So what does it all mean?
Doctor: Your HIV remains well controlled on Biktarvy. The diarrhea sounds like traveler's diarrhea that resolved with azithromycin, and since you have no fever and finished your malaria prophylaxis, I don't need any malaria testing. Your hypertension was above goal on both readings today, so I'm going to increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg once a day and recheck your kidney function and potassium in two weeks. Keep taking atorvastatin 20 milligrams. Your reflux has settled, so let's stop the omeprazole. If you need an antacid like Tums again, take it with your Biktarvy only when you eat, or take the Biktarvy at least two hours before it. We'll do your routine sexually transmitted infection screening today with a syphilis blood test and urine tests, and give you your flu shot. Please keep a blood pressure log at home.
Patient: Sounds good.
Doctor: I'll see you in three months with repeat labs. Come in sooner if you get a fever or any new symptoms.

She describes about two months of low mood, loss of interest in activities, poor sleep, low energy, and trouble concentrating that began after she lost her job. Telehealth video visit, neurology follow-up for persistent symptoms after a concussion. The patient is a 37-year-old male connecting from home on a smartphone with good audio and video, and he agreed to a video visit after we discussed its limits. His sister helped him open the link. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, short steps, and teach-back, and I asked him to hold each pill bottle up to the camera so we could read the labels together.

He fell off his bicycle 6 weeks ago and hit his head on the pavement. He did not lose consciousness, and a head CT in the emergency department that day showed no bleeding or fracture. Since then he has had daily headaches that feel like a tight band, worse in the afternoon and when he looks at screens, along with dizziness when he turns his head quickly, sensitivity to light, trouble concentrating at work, poor sleep, and irritability. He denies vomiting, double vision, weakness, numbness, seizures, neck pain, and new confusion, and the headaches are not getting worse. He denies thoughts of harming himself.

His history includes migraine without aura since his twenties, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP most nights, and acid reflux. When I asked about his blood pressure pill he first said lisinopril 20 mg daily, but when he held up the bottle he read it as lisinopril 10 mg daily, so the correct dose is 10 mg daily. He also takes omeprazole 20 mg every morning for reflux, sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine, which he has used once since the injury, and amitriptyline 10 mg at bedtime, which another provider started 3 weeks ago for sleep and headache. For the past 5 weeks he has also taken ibuprofen 400 mg three to four times a day for the headaches. He has no known drug allergies.

He measured these at home with his own cuff during the visit: blood pressure 128/82, heart rate 76, and temperature 36.8 C. On video he looks comfortable, is alert, speaks fluently, and follows multi-step commands. He squints in the room light but has no facial droop. His eye movements look full and smooth, finger-to-nose testing was accurate on both sides, and he walked in a straight line with a steady turn. I could not do a fundus exam or check reflexes over video. A PHQ-9 read aloud to him was 6, which is mild. Labs from his primary clinic 2 months ago showed TSH 1.9 and hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL.

My impression is post-concussion syndrome after a mild head injury, with headaches, dizziness, light sensitivity, and sleep problems, and with a risk of medication-overuse headache from near-daily ibuprofen. His hypertension looks controlled on the home reading, and his migraine and OSA are stable. For the plan, I told him to stop ibuprofen completely because daily use can make headaches worse and raise blood pressure. He should take no pain pills on more than 2 days a week, and on those days he may take acetaminophen 500 mg. I increased amitriptyline from 10 mg to 25 mg at bedtime. He will continue lisinopril 10 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg every morning, sumatriptan 50 mg as needed, and CPAP nightly. I referred him to vestibular physical therapy for the dizziness. He should rest from cycling and sports until cleared, take a screen break every 20 minutes, and keep a regular sleep schedule, and I gave him a work note for reduced hours for 2 weeks. I asked him to mark headache days on a simple calendar, and he repeated the plan back correctly. Video follow-up in 3 weeks. Doctor: Hi, I have you down as a 48-year-old female with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump. What brought you in today?
Patient: My blood sugar keeps dropping too low and I'm really worried. This morning I got shaky and sweaty, and my meter said 54. I drank some juice, but I'm scared it will happen again. Is my pump broken?
Doctor: Good question. How often have the lows been happening?
Patient: Maybe three times a week for the past month, usually in the middle of the afternoon. Should I turn the pump off? Can a low damage my brain? Should I go to the hospital?
Doctor: Those are all fair questions. Have you passed out or had a seizure when you were low?
Patient: No, I've never passed out and I haven't had a seizure. I always catch it before that.
Doctor: Any chest pain or vomiting today?
Patient: No chest pain and no vomiting. I feel clear-headed now.
Doctor: Good. I checked a fingerstick glucose here and it is 112 after the juice. Your blood pressure is 122/74 and your heart rate is 80. The pump site on your belly looks clean with no redness, and the pump is working normally, so it does not look broken.
Patient: So what is going on? And will the lows hurt my brain?
Doctor: Lows treated quickly do not damage the brain, and you do not need the hospital today. I think the insulin lispro your pump gives in the afternoon is too much. Your basal rate from noon to 4 p.m. is 0.85 units per hour, and I am lowering it to 0.7 units per hour. I am also prescribing nasal glucagon 3 mg to keep at home for a severe low, and I will show you how to use it.
Patient: Okay, lower the afternoon rate and get the nasal glucagon. Should I keep checking my sugar?
Doctor: Yes, keep your low alert at 70 and send your pump readings to the endocrinology clinic. You will see them in one week. If you ever pass out or cannot treat a low, call 911.
Patient: Thank you, that makes me feel a lot better.
summary: A 48-year-old female with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump came to urgent care worried about low blood sugars about three times a week, including a morning meter reading of 54 with shakiness and sweating. The impression is recurrent afternoon hypoglycemia from too much basal insulin, not a broken pump. The afternoon basal rate was lowered from 0.85 to 0.7 units per hour, nasal glucagon was prescribed, and endocrinology follow-up is in one week.

Dermatology clinic follow-up for a 48-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis treated with adalimumab, seen for a flare. She was diagnosed about 5 years ago and has had a good response to adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for the past 18 months, with clear skin until about 2 months ago. Over the past 6 weeks the plaques have returned on her elbows, knees, lower back, and scalp with itching, and her fingernails have started to pit again. She traveled in Southeast Asia for 3 weeks and returned 10 days ago. When I asked about her last injection she first said it was 2 weeks ago, but after checking her pharmacy app she corrected herself: her last adalimumab dose was 5 weeks ago, because she left her pens behind during the trip and missed two doses. The last dose was therefore 5 weeks ago, not 2.

She reports mild traveler's diarrhea early in the trip that resolved on its own without antibiotics. She denies fever, cough, night sweats, weight loss, joint pain, joint swelling, and any new rash outside her psoriasis, and no one at home is sick. She received no vaccines before the trip.

Her other conditions are hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. Her medicines are lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily to the plaques, which has not helped, and calcipotriene-betamethasone foam, which she has been using only twice a week on her scalp. Pregnancy status matters for prescribing: she uses a copper IUD for contraception, her urine pregnancy test today was negative, and she is not planning a pregnancy. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam, blood pressure is 136/84, heart rate 74, temperature 36.7 C, and weight 86 kg. She has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on both elbows, both knees, the lower back, and the scalp, with pitting of four fingernails. The body surface area involved is about 8% and the PASI score is 9.2. There is no joint swelling, no dactylitis, no lymphadenopathy, and no sign of skin infection. Labs today show ALT 24, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, WBC 6.4, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, A1c 6.8%, and LDL 118 mg/dL. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold was negative 11 months ago, and a chest x-ray at that time was normal.

Impression: a flare of moderate plaque psoriasis after missed adalimumab doses during travel, with no sign of infection and a negative pregnancy test. Because of her recent travel to an area where tuberculosis is more common, I will repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold today before she resumes the biologic. I considered adding methotrexate or acitretin but will not start either because of the risk to a pregnancy, and her skin should not need a systemic add-on once the biologic is resumed. For the plan, stop the triamcinolone cream. Start clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily to the body plaques for up to 2 weeks, not on the face or skin folds. Change the calcipotriene-betamethasone foam from twice a week to once daily on the scalp for 4 weeks. Resume adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks, with the next dose once the QuantiFERON-TB Gold result is back and negative, and no loading dose. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Avoid live vaccines while on adalimumab. She should call for fever, cough, or a skin infection. Return in 8 weeks to repeat the PASI score.
summary: A 48-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis on adalimumab presented with a flare after missing two doses during a 3-week trip to Southeast Asia, with the last dose 5 weeks ago. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, uses a copper IUD, and had a negative urine pregnancy test. Plaques cover about 8% of the body surface with a PASI of 9.2, and there are no signs of infection or joint involvement. Triamcinolone was stopped, clobetasol was started, and the scalp foam was increased to daily. Adalimumab will resume after a repeat QuantiFERON-TB Gold is negative, and methotrexate and acitretin were avoided because of pregnancy risk.
